Glossary

New words from all three levels, in plain language. The label tells you which week you first meet the word. Words in this font are typed exactly like that in Python.

  • Level 1: Introduction
  • Level 2: Intermediate
  • Level 3: Advanced

Level 1: Introduction

  • A
  • B
  • C
  • D
  • E
  • F
  • G
  • I
  • L
  • M
  • N
  • O
  • P
  • R
  • S
  • T
  • V

A

accessibility W5
Making things that everyone can use, including people who see colors differently or need bigger text.
Example: Using color-blind-safe colors and also different shapes.
accessible W5
Easy for everyone to use, including people who see or hear differently.
algorithm W1
A list of exact steps, in the right order, that solves a problem or does a job.
Example: A recipe for a sandwich.
angle W2
How far you turn, measured in degrees. A full turn is 360 degrees. A shape with nn sides turns 360÷n360 \div n at each corner.
Example: A square turns 90 degrees at each corner.

B

backdrop W1
The picture behind everything on the Scratch stage.
broadcast W5
A Scratch message sent to every sprite. Sprites with a matching “when I receive” block start running.
Example: “broadcast start game”.
bug W1
A mistake in a program that makes it do something we did not want. Bugs are normal: every programmer meets them every day.
Example: The turtle turns 90 instead of 120.
bug / debugging W1
A mistake in a program / finding and fixing it.

C

call W10
To use a function, by writing its name with brackets.
Example: house(0, 0, ORANGE) calls the function house.
checkpoint W6
A short check that shows what you know and what to practice next.
color code W9
A color written as # and six letters or numbers, so the computer knows exactly which color you mean.
Example: "#0072B2" is blue.
comment W7
A note for humans in the code. Python ignores it. In Python it starts with #.
Example: # draw the roof
comparison W9
A question that is True or False, made with >> (bigger), << (smaller), == (equal) or != (not equal).
Example: stars > 5
conditional W3
Code that only runs if something is true. Also called an if.
Example: “If touching the edge, then bounce.”
coordinates W1
Two numbers, xx and yy, that give a place on the screen. xx is left–right, yy is down–up. The middle is (0,0)(0, 0).
Example: t.goto(200, 150)
costume W2
One of the pictures a Scratch sprite can wear. Switching costumes quickly makes animation.
credit W4
Saying who made the art, sounds or ideas you used. It is fair and kind.
Example: “Cat sounds from the Scratch library.”

D

debug W1
To find a bug and fix it. A good strategy: read the error, check the last thing you changed, test one small part at a time.
debugging W6
Finding and fixing bugs, step by step, like a detective.
decomposition W5
Breaking a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
Example: A house = walls + roof + door + windows.
def W10
The Python word that starts a new function (your own command).
Example: def square(size):
Demo W12
Short for demonstration: running your program and showing how it works.
driver W1
In pair programming, the person using the mouse and keyboard.
driver / navigator W1
The driver clicks; the navigator reads, checks and helps.

E

Editor W7
The top part of Thonny where you write your program.
elif W9
Short for “else if”: another question to check when the first if was false.
Example: elif n == 10:
else W3
The part of an if that runs when the question is false.
error message W7
The red text Python shows when it cannot run your code. It tells you the line number and a clue.
Example: NameError: name ’Print’ is not defined
event W3
Something that happens and starts code running.
Example: Clicking the green flag, pressing a key.
extension W2
Extra blocks you can add to Scratch, like the Pen.

F

feedback W3
Helpful comments about someone’s work. We use “two stars and a wish”: two things you like, one idea to improve.
Feedback card W12
A card with two stars and a wish for an artist.
for loop W8
Python’s repeat block. The lines pushed in underneath it are repeated.
Example: for i in range(4):
forever W2
A Scratch loop that never stops (until you click the red stop sign).
function W10
A named set of steps you can use again and again. Python’s version of a My Block.
Example: square(50)

G

green flag W1
The Scratch button that starts a project.

I

if W3
A block or line that asks a question and only runs its steps when the answer is true.
Example: if mood == "happy":
if / elif / else W9
Python’s way to choose: “if this, else if that, otherwise…”
if-else W3
Runs one set of blocks for yes and another for no.
indentation W8
Spaces at the start of a line (4 in Python). They show which lines are inside a loop, an if or a function.
input W9
Information that goes into a program, often typed by the user. In Python input() asks a question and gives back the answer as text.
Example: answer = input("How many? ")
integer (int) W9
A whole number, like 3, 0 or −7-7. int() turns text like "5" into the number 5.
Example: n = int(answer)
Iterate W11
To improve something by going round the build–run–check loop again and again.

L

loop W2
Code that repeats. Loops save you writing the same steps again and again.
Example: repeat 4, for i in range(4):

M

Milestone W11
A checkpoint on the way to finishing a project.
My Block W5
A block you make yourself in Scratch with “Make a Block”. It can have inputs.
Example: “define flower (size)”

N

navigator W1
In pair programming, the person who reads the instructions, thinks ahead and spots bugs.
nested loop W8
A loop inside another loop.
Example: Repeat 6 times: draw a square.

O

Off-by-one bug W8
When a loop runs one time too many or one time too few.
output W7
What a program shows or does: text, a drawing, a sound.

P

pair programming W1
Two people coding together on one computer: a driver and a navigator who swap roles.
parameter W5
An input that a My Block or function needs. It makes the block flexible.
Example: In square(size), size is a parameter.
pen W2
Lets a sprite or turtle draw a line where it moves. Pen up: no line. Pen down: draw.
pixel B1
One tiny square of color. Screens make pictures out of millions of pixels.
playtest W11
Letting someone try your program so you can see what works and what confuses them.
print W7
The Python command that shows text in the Shell.
Example: print("Hello!")
privacy W1
Keeping personal information (real name, address, school, photos, passwords) safe. We use nicknames.
program W1
A set of instructions a computer follows.
Python W7
A programming language where you type words instead of dragging blocks.

R

random W4
Picked by chance, so you cannot guess it. Great for surprises and games.
Example: random.randint(1, 6), “pick random 1 to 6”
range W8
Tells a for loop how many times to repeat.
Example: range(5) repeats 5 times.
Reflection W12
Thinking back about what you did, what you learned and what you want next.
remix W4
Making something new from someone else’s work, and giving them credit.
repeat W2
A Scratch loop that runs the blocks inside a set number of times.
run W1
To start a program. In Thonny, the green Run button or .

S

script W1
A stack of Scratch blocks that are joined together.
sensing W3
Scratch blocks that check things, like “touching edge?” or “key space pressed?”.
sequence W1
Steps that happen one after another, in order. Order matters!
Shell W7
The part of Thonny at the bottom where print shows text and you type answers.
Showcase W12
An event where you show your work to others.
sprite W1
A character or object in Scratch that you can program.
Example: The Scratch cat.
stage W1
The area in Scratch where the sprites move and the project plays.
string W9
Text in a program, written inside quotes. input() always gives a string.
Example: "day", "25"
syntax W7
The spelling and grammar rules of a programming language.
syntax error W7
An error because the code breaks Python’s rules, like a missing bracket or colon.
Example: print("hi"

T

test W7
Running a program on purpose to check that it works. check_my_work.py runs tests for you.
text code W6
Code made of typed words and symbols.
Thonny W7
The app we use to write and run Python.
turtle W7
A Python drawing tool: an arrow you move around the screen that draws lines.
Example: t = turtle.Turtle()

V

variable W4
A labeled box that remembers a value, like a score or an answer. The value can change.
Example: score = 0

I

.items() W5
Gives every key together with its value, so a loop can use both.
index W3
The position of an item in a list. The first item has index 0.
IndexError W3
The error you get when you ask for an index that is not in the list.
infinite loop W4
A loop that never stops. Press the red Stop button.
input validation W4
Checking that what the user typed makes sense, and asking again if not.
int W1
The type for whole numbers like 7 or −3-3.
item W3
One value inside a list. Also called an element.

A

accessibility W11
designing so that everyone can use it, including people who see colors differently or read more slowly.
accessible W3
Designed so that everyone can use it, including people who see colors differently.
and W1
Joins two conditions. Both must be True: score > 5 and lives > 0.
append W3
Adds an item to the end of a list: names.append("Zoe").
argument W2
The value you put in the brackets when you call a function. In area(3, 4) the arguments are 3 and 4.
assert W8
Checks that something is True. If it is not, the test fails and shows your message.
attribution W9
Saying who made the art, sound or code you used. Giving credit.

B

bool W1
The type for True or False.
break W4
Leaves a loop straight away.
bug
A mistake in a program. Every programmer makes them; finding them is part of the fun.
bug list W11
a list of problems found in testing, sorted so the most important ones get fixed first.
bug report W6
A short note: what went wrong, where, and what you changed.

C

Caesar cipher W5
A secret code that shifts every letter along the alphabet by the same amount.
code review W10
Reading someone’s code to ask questions, find bugs and say what is good.
collision W9
When two things in a game touch. We check it with distance.
comment W2
A note for people, after a #. Python ignores it.
compound condition W1
Two or more conditions joined with and, or or not.
core loop W10
the part of a game or app that repeats over and over; the smallest version that works.

D

data privacy W7
Deciding what information about people is saved, who can see it, and keeping it safe.
data type W1
The kind of value: int, float, str or bool. Also just called a type.
debugging W6
Finding and fixing bugs with a strategy: read the traceback, print-debugging, rubber duck.
decomposition W10
Breaking a big problem into small parts you can solve one at a time.
design decision W12
a choice you made on purpose, and the reason for it.
dictionary (dict) W5
A collection that stores values under names (keys): {"lives": 3}.
docstring W2
A comment in triple quotes as the first line of a function, saying what it does.
driver
In pair programming, the person at the keyboard.

E

edge case W8
A test at the very edge of what is allowed: zero, an empty list, a wall.
encode / decode W5
Turn a message into secret code / turn it back again.
encryption W5
Scrambling a message so only people with the key can read it.
event W9
Something that happens, like a key press, a click or a timer going off.
event handler W9
The function that runs when an event happens.
expected vs actual W8
What the test says should happen, and what really happened.

F

f-string W1
A string with an f in front that fills in values: f"Score: {score}".
file W7
Data saved on the computer, so it is still there after the program stops.
FileNotFoundError W7
The error you get when you try to read a file that does not exist (yet).
float W1
The type for decimal numbers like 3.5.
flowchart W10
A drawing of a program’s steps with boxes and arrows.
frame W9
One tiny step of a game: everything moves a little, then it is drawn.
function W2
A named block of code you can use again. Made with def.

G

gallery walk W12
visiting projects one by one, like in a museum, and leaving feedback.
game loop W4, 9
The part of a game that runs again and again: move, check, draw.
game state W9
All the values that describe the game right now: score, lives, positions.

K

key W5
The name you use to look up a value in a dictionary.
KeyError W5
The error you get when a key is not in the dictionary. Check the spelling!

L

len W3
Tells you how many items are in a list (or letters in a string).
license / attribution W9
The rules for using someone’s work / giving them credit for it.
list W3
A collection of values in order: ["red", "blue"].
listen W9
Makes the turtle window pay attention to the keyboard.

M

milestone W10
a checkpoint on the way to the finished project, like M2 “core loop works”.
mode W7
How a file is opened: "r" read, "w" write (starts empty), "a" append (adds to the end).

N

navigator
In pair programming, the person who reads the task, thinks ahead and spots bugs.
nested loop W4
A loop inside another loop. Great for grids and pixel art.
None W2
Python’s word for “nothing”. A function with no return gives back None.
normal case W8
A test with ordinary, everyday values.
not W1
Turns True into False and False into True.

O

off-by-one W3
A bug where a number is one too big or one too small, like using len as the last index.
onkey W9
Tells turtle which function to run when a key is pressed.
ontimer W9
Tells turtle to run a function after some milliseconds.
open / with W7
open gets a file ready to use; with closes it again automatically.
open license W9
Permission from a creator that lets others use their work, often if they give credit.
or W1
Joins two conditions. At least one must be True.

P

parameter W2
A name in a function’s brackets that receives a value: def area(width, height).
personal information W1
Anything that tells who or where you are: real name, address, school, birthday, photos.
pitch W12
a short talk that explains what your project is and why it is interesting.
playtest W11
Letting someone try your game while you watch and take notes.
polish W11
small finishing touches that make a working program clearer and nicer to use.
print-debugging W6
Adding print lines to see what your variables hold.
pseudocode W10
Planning a program in plain words before writing Python.
pytest W8
A tool that finds your test_ functions and runs them all.

R

random.choice W3
Picks one random item from a list.
read / write / append W7
The modes "r", "w" and "a": look, replace everything, or add to the end.
return W2
Hands a value back from a function to the code that called it.
return value W2
The value a function hands back.
rubber duck debugging W6
Explaining your code line by line out loud (to a toy or a friend) until you spot the bug.

S

scope W2
Where a variable can be used. Variables made inside a function stay inside it.
showcase W12
an event where makers show their work and explain it.
split W7
Cuts a string into a list of words: "a b".split() gives ["a", "b"].
str (string) W1
The type for text, written in quotes: "hello".
strip W7
Removes spaces and new-line characters from both ends of a string.

T

test W8
A small function that checks your code works, using assert.
trace table W6
A table on paper where you write how variables change, step by step.
traceback W6
The error report Python shows. Read the last line first.
TypeError W1
The error you get when you mix types that do not fit, like "5" + 5.

V

value W1, 5
A piece of data, like 7, "hi" or True. In a dictionary, what is stored under a key.
variable W1
A name that stores a value. Choose clear names like lives, not x.
version W12
one stage of a project; version 2 is the next, improved one.

W

while loop W4
Repeats while a condition is True. Something inside must change so it can stop.
with W7
Opens a file and closes it again safely when the block ends.

I

__init__ W2
The method that runs when a new object is made. It sets the starting attributes.
inheritance W3
When a class gets all the code of a parent class and adds or changes some: a Knight is a Character.

A

accessibility W11
Designing so that people with different abilities can use it too.
accuracy W9
Correct guesses divided by the number of test examples.
algorithm W4
A precise list of steps that solves a problem, like a recipe. Binary search and selection sort are famous ones.
anonymize W8
Remove or replace anything that could show who gave an answer.
attribute W2
A value stored inside an object, such as self.name or self.energy. What an object has.
average (mean) W8
Add up all the numbers and divide by how many there are.

B

base case W7
The part of a recursive function that stops it from calling itself again. Without one you get a RecursionError.
bias W9
When data or a program treats some people or things unfairly, often because the training data left some of them out.
binary search W4
Searching a sorted list by checking the middle and throwing away the half that cannot hold the answer. Very fast.
breadth-first search (BFS) W7
Exploring a maze in rings, one step further each time, using a queue. It finds a shortest path.
breakpoint W6
A marked line where the debugger pauses.
bubble sort W5
Sorting by swapping neighbors that are in the wrong order, again and again.

C

class W2
A blueprint for making objects. It lists their attributes and methods.
class diagram W10
A drawing of the classes in a program, their attributes and methods, and how they are connected.
classifier W9
A program that puts things into groups (labels), such as “dragon” or “slime”.
clean (data) W8
Fix messy data before using it: remove empty rows, strip spaces, turn text into numbers.
code of conduct W12
The rules a community agrees to, so everyone stays safe and respected.
code review W10
Reading someone’s code to find bugs and suggest improvements, kindly.
commit W1
A save point in git, with a message saying what changed.
commit id W1
The short code name of a commit, like a1b2c3d.
commit message W1
A short label that says what changed, like “Add jump to hero”.
composition W3
Building an object out of other objects: a Game has a Maze and a Player.
consent W8
Agreeing, freely, to take part – with the choice to say no.
CRC card W10
A paper card for designing a class: its name (Class), its jobs (Responsibilities) and who it works with (Collaborators).
CSV W8
“Comma-separated values”: a table saved as plain text, one row per line, commas between columns.

D

data cleaning W8
Fixing messy data (spaces, capitals, missing or empty values) before using it.
data structure W5
A way of organizing data in a program: a list, dictionary, stack, queue or grid.
debugger W6
A tool (the bug button in Thonny) that runs your program one step at a time so you can watch the variables.
deepfake W9
A fake picture, video or voice made by AI to look real.
deque W5
“Double-ended queue” from collections. Fast to add at the back and take from the front with popleft().
design decision W12
A choice about how to build something, with a reason.
diff W1
The lines that changed between two versions. git diff shows them.

E

edge case W11
An unusual input that can break a program, such as an empty list. Good tests try edge cases.

F

feature (AI) W9
A number that describes an example, such as size or number of spikes. Classifiers compare features.
feedback W12
Comments that help someone improve: kind, specific, useful.
flood fill W7
Filling every connected square of the same kind, like the paint bucket tool. Usually written with recursion.
fractal W7
A pattern made of smaller copies of itself, like a tree whose branches look like little trees.

G

git W1
A program that keeps save points (commits) of a folder so you can see and undo changes.
grid (2D list) W7
A list of lists, like a chessboard: grid[row][col].

H

header W8
The first line of a CSV file, with the column names.

K

key function W5
A function that tells sorted what to sort by.

L

license W10
The rules that say how you may use someone’s code, pictures or sounds.
linear search W4
Checking items one by one from the start until you find what you want.

M

Markov text generator W9
A program that writes new text by choosing each next word from the words that followed it in its training text.
method W2
A function that belongs to a class. What an object does.
milestone W10
A checkpoint in a project plan, with a date and a list of what should work.

N

nearest neighbor W9
An AI method: label a mystery item with the label of the most similar training example.

O

object (instance) W2
One thing made from a class: mo = Pet("Mo") makes one pet.
off-by-one error W4
A bug where a number is 1 too big or 1 too small, like using < instead of <=.
override W3
Writing a method in a child class with the same name as in the parent class, to change what it does.

P

parent class / child class W3
The general class and the more special class built from it. Also called superclass and subclass.
playtest W11
Watching someone use your project to find problems.
polymorphism W3
Different classes answering the same method call in their own way.

Q

queue W5
First in, first out, like a lunch line.

R

README W11
A file that explains what a project is, how to run it and how it is built.
recursion W7
When a function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
RecursionError W7
Python’s error when a function calls itself too many times, usually because the base case is missing.
recursive case W7
The part that does a small step and calls the function on a smaller problem.
repository (repo) W1
A folder that git is tracking, with all its save points.
restore W1
git restore file.py throws away changes you have not committed yet.

S

sample W8
The group of people who answered. A small sample can give misleading results.
selection sort W5
Sorting by finding the smallest item and swapping it to the front, then repeating with the rest.
self W2
Inside a method, the object the method was called on.
showcase W12
An event where makers show and explain their work.
stack W5
Last in, first out, like a pile of plates or an undo button.
step into W6
Go inside the function or method that the line calls.
step over W6
Run the highlighted line in one go, then pause.
super() W3
Calls the parent class’s version of a method, often super().__init__(…).

T

Terminal W1
The Mac app where you type commands such as git status.
test data W9
Examples kept secret during training, used to check the guesses.
trace table W6
A paper table where you write each variable’s value, step by step.
traceback W6
The error report Python prints. Read it from the bottom.
training data W9
The labeled examples an AI learns from.
triage W11
Sorting problems by how much they matter, to fix the important ones first.

U

usability W11
How easy something is to use for someone new.

V

version 2 W12
The next, improved release of a project.

W

worst case W4
The unluckiest situation, when an algorithm needs the most steps.

Kids Coding

A free course for children from Grade 5: make games and art, first with Scratch blocks, then with Python. One 60-minute session a week.

No accounts, no ads, no tracking.
